atlas-il.0135: There is no internship visa, and an internship on an ETA-IL is illegal work. Students enrolled in Israel may do a required placement; otherwise a company must hire you on a B/1, or you join an accredited Masa Israel programme (ages 18 to 35) on an A/2.
atlas-il.0136: Hi-tech route for Israeli STEM graduates
atlas-il.0137: There is no post-study visa. The one exception: companies certified by the Innovation Authority can hire graduates of Israeli universities in tech fields without the double-average-wage rule, for three years after graduating, within 500 permits a year. A European degree does not qualify.
atlas-il.0139: The employer must pay a base salary of at least twice the national average, with no bonuses or allowances counted; one year at a time, up to 63 months. Ordinary jobs below that level are closed to foreigners.
atlas-il.0140: Tech companies certified by the Innovation Authority get a decision in 6 to 10 working days, and the spouse gets an open work permit.
atlas-il.0141: For tasks of up to 90 days a year, the STEP route skips the salary rule for visa-exempt nationals.
atlas-il.0145: The employer may not pass these fees on to you; spouses of ordinary experts may not work.
atlas-il.0146: Visiting researchers, post-docs and PhD students on a fellowship hold an A/2, and fellowships from recognised institutions are free of income tax. Researchers on an employment contract hold a B/1.
atlas-il.0147: Weizmann, Technion, Tel Aviv and Hebrew University offer international PhD students full packages with a stipend and no tuition.
atlas-il.0148: Only for Germans, Austrians and Czechs among EU citizens (plus Australians, New Zealanders and South Koreans): aged 18 to 30, up to 12 months, at most three months per employer. Italy and other EU countries have no agreement.
atlas-il.0149: Israel has no working-holiday agreement with the UK.
atlas-il.0150: Since 1 January 2025 visa-exempt visitors need an ETA-IL before boarding: valid two years, up to 90 days a visit, with no work, internship or formal study.
atlas-il.0151: Visitors need the electronic travel authorisation ETA-IL before flying. At Ben Gurion, security officers may ask to see your phone, chats and social media, and past travel to Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq or Yemen triggers long extra checks.
atlas-il.0152: Israel does not stamp passports: at the border you get a light-blue slip (Form 294) with your visa category, the only proof that your stay is legal. Keep it in your passport until you leave and photograph it straight away.
atlas-il.0153: Israeli banks (Hapoalim, Leumi, Discount) are built around the 9-digit citizen ID number, which B/1 and A/2 visa holders do not have: there is no online onboarding, so go to a branch with an international desk.
atlas-il.0154: Work (B/1) and student (A/2) visas are single-entry: before any trip abroad, apply through the MyVisit app 21 to 30 days ahead for a re-entry visa (inter-visa, 205 NIS), or the visa lapses as you leave. Emergency extensions in wartime do not count as one.
atlas-il.0155: B/1 and A/2 visas are single-entry: leave without a re-entry permit, requested 21 to 30 days ahead, and the visa is cancelled at the border. Automatic wartime extensions do not count as one.
atlas-il.0156: Passports are not stamped: the blue entry slip is your only proof of legal stay. Keep it until you leave.
atlas-il.0157: Security staff at Ben Gurion may ask to see phones and social media; past travel to Iran, Lebanon, Syria, Iraq, Yemen or the West Bank means long questioning.
atlas-il.0158: Without an Israeli ID number you cannot open a bank account online: it takes a branch with an international desk.
atlas-il.0159: The 2026 B/1 fees come from a secondary source; the official table could not be read.
atlas-il.0160: Whether the 500 permits for Israeli STEM graduates run out during the year.
atlas-il.0161: Consular appointments in Rome for B/1 and A/2 visas take 2 to 8 weeks.
